questions.explanation: While some energy is absorbed by the isolator material (damping), this is secondary; the primary mechanism is frequency separation (tuning). Pure energy absorption would be inefficient. Raising the natural frequency would bring it closer to equipment vibration, reducing isolation effectiveness and potentially creating resonance amplification. Isolators are designed for selective frequency isolation, not flat damping; equal attenuation across all frequencies is neither achievable nor desired. Vibration isolation works by setting the system natural frequency (f_n) well below the equipment vibration frequency (f_e). When f_e >> f_n (typically f_e > 2.5 × f_n), attenuation ∝ (f_e/f_n)². At 2–5 Hz natural frequency with equipment vibration at 30+ Hz, this produces 20–30 dB reduction (CIBSE Guide E; ASHRAE). Effective vibration isolation requires frequency separation: f_n << f_e, not mass increase or frequency matching.
questions.code_citation: ASHRAE Handbook—Fundamentals (2021), Chapter 43 (Vibration Isolation); CIBSE Guide E (2018)

questions.explanation: This reverses the definitions; NC is spectral, dB(A) is overall single-number. While both metrics can be measured simultaneously, NC and dB(A) capture different aspects of the acoustic environment. NC 30 might correspond to dB(A) 40–45 depending on spectral content. Both metrics apply to indoor and outdoor environments. NC is typically used for enclosed spaces; dB(A) is the legal standard for environmental/property boundary compliance (DENR DAO 2000-81). NC (ANSI/ASA S12.2-2008) is a spectral criterion providing acceptable sound levels across 11 octave bands (63 Hz–8 kHz), designed to correlate with speech intelligibility and task performance in specific room types. dB(A) is an overall sound pressure level weighted by the A-weighting curve (ISO 226), reducing low-frequency sensitivity. A design can meet NC 30 in one space and dB(A) 45 in another; NC captures spectral balance (avoiding low-frequency dominance), while dB(A) represents overall energy. ASHRAE design typically specifies both: NC for spectral compliance in occupied spaces, dB(A) for overall budget in mechanical areas. Design specifications must address both NC (spectral quality) and dB(A) (overall energy); meeting one does not guarantee the other, particularly if low-frequency energy dominates.
